Exploring Biomass Data
for the Itombwe Forest

open satellite biomass data for Itombwe — comparing two datasets and working out what they suggest about the forest's carbon.

Itombwe

From Ctree's 100m Above Ground Biomass (AGB) data (2000-2025).

What stands out: There's a dense, high-biomass core (the darker greens) that looks like intact rainforest — densest in the southwest (the Wamuzimu and Basile sectors) — wrapped in lighter areas, likely degraded, farmed, or cleared land, that thin out toward the eastern and northeastern edges (the Bafuliiru lowland reads lowest).

That pattern points to where the forest seems healthy versus where the pressure is, straight from satellite + AI with no ground survey. Whether the pale zones are genuine degradation or just naturally lower vegetation is something we'd want to confirm on the ground.

Change over time (2000–2025)

CTrees covers 2000–2025, so we can watch the forest change rather than rely on a single snapshot.

Year to year, the maps look almost identical. Average density drifts from about 147 to 145 Mg/ha — the -0.06%/yr we see in the trend (-1.4% over the full period). Real, but small enough to miss on a map.

So a snapshot hides the story. To see where the forest is actually under pressure, it helps to map the change itself rather than the biomass — that's the panel below.

Key Findings About 27% of the reserve shows a net biomass loss, concentrated along the eastern and northeastern edges and the farmed/settled frontier — exactly where rangers, satellite alerts, and cookstove/livelihood programs would go first.

Note: at ~100 m, the change in any single pixel carries model noise, so read the clusters as the signal rather than individual pixels. The hotspots are worth confirming against GFW GLAD/RADD alerts and on the ground.

Helpful Glossary

Biomass — the living plant matter (trunks, branches, leaves). More biomass = more carbon stored.
Mg/ha (tonnes per hectare) — how dense the biomass is. A hectare is ~2.5 acres.
Carbon stock — how much carbon the forest is holding right now.
CO₂e — that carbon expressed as tonnes of CO₂; the unit carbon markets trade in.
REDD+ — a framework where forests earn money for the emissions avoided by not being cleared.
Carbon credit — one tonne of CO₂ kept out of the air; buyers purchase these to offset their own emissions.

Reading it: Wamuzimu and Itombwe together hold roughly three-quarters of the reserve's above-ground carbon. The steepest proportional losses sit in the smaller, more accessible edge sectors — useful for targeting patrols and livelihood programs.

Biomass dataset comparison — CTrees vs. Chloris

There are several open satellite biomass products. I pulled two and compared them over Itombwe: CTrees (fine, ~100 m pixels) and Chloris (coarse, ~4.6 km pixels). They give noticeably different pictures.

What I looked atChloris (~4.6 km)CTrees (~100 m)
Resolution over the reserve~270 pixels~590,000 pixels
Mean biomass density~214 Mg/ha~145 Mg/ha
Implied carbon stock~220 M tonnes CO₂e~145 M tonnes CO₂e
Trend, 2000–2025roughly flata slight decline
Why they differ so much. It's mostly resolution. Coarse pixels average small clearings and degraded edges together with healthy forest into one number; fine pixels keep them separate, so CTrees reads lower. Worth settling on which dataset fits Itombwe best.
(CTrees numbers are now clipped to the exact reserve polygon; the Chloris figures are scaled from the earlier read and worth re-clipping too.)

Biomass over time

Across 2000–2025 the reserve's carbon stock drifts gently downward — about -1.4% over the period (-0.06% a year).

Small but steady, and in the direction you'd expect if slow logging and charcoal/fuelwood pressure are nibbling at the forest. The coarser dataset showed this same forest as basically flat.

Deforestation — the activity data — GFW / Hansen vs CTrees

Carbon credits aren't paid on biomass density — they're paid on forest actually cleared. For that we pulled the Hansen Global Forest Change tree-cover-loss layer (the UMD/Landsat ~30 m product that Global Forest Watch redistributes — "GFW loss" is Hansen) and clipped it to the reserve.

25,097 ha
Cleared 2001–2024
4.4% of the reserve's 2000 forest
~1,616 ha/yr
Recent rate (2015–24)
Up from ~500 ha/yr in the 2000s — accelerating
~68 Mg/ha
Biomass at cleared sites
Roughly half the reserve mean — clearing hits the accessible edges
Why GFW and CTrees seem to disagree. They measure different things and both are right. GFW counts gross canopy removal at 30 m; CTrees tracks net biomass at 100 m, where regrowth and the coarser pixels offset much of the loss. So CTrees reads a gentle −1.4% while GFW shows 4.4% of the forest cleared and accelerating. For crediting, the cleared area (GFW) is the activity data Verra wants; CTrees supplies the carbon-per-hectare.

What it might be worth — Verra VM0048 / VMD0055

How a project earns credits — and the formula Verra actually uses

  1. The forest is being cleared every year — for farmland, charcoal and fuelwood — releasing the carbon in those trees. A protection effort (rangers and patrols, improved cookstoves and livelihoods, satellite alerts) lowers that rate. Each tonne of CO₂ kept in the trees earns one carbon credit; buyers purchase them to offset emissions, and that money funds the protection.
  2. Verra's REDD methodology — VM0048 with its unplanned-deforestation module VMD0055 — does not credit an average biomass-decline rate. It uses Activity Data × Emission Factor: the area of forest cleared per year × the carbon released per hectare. That's the calculation below — built from the GFW clearing rate (AD) and the CTrees biomass at each cleared site in the year before it was cleared (EF), summed per annual cohort.
Interim estimate. A fully compliant VM0048 baseline reads its deforestation rate from a Verra jurisdictional risk map — which is not yet published for South Kivu (only DR Congo's Mai Ndombe region is near completion). So we use our own GFW-measured clearing rate as a stand-in, and the effectiveness / leakage / uncertainty / buffer factors are illustrative placeholders a registry-approved method would set.

On this basis the estimate lands around ~69,436 credits a year. The chain is the VM0048 formula, one factor at a time:

StepWhat it doesRunning total
Activity data (AD)forest cleared per year (GFW/Hansen, 2015–24 mean) 1,616 ha/yr
× EF = 145 tCO₂e/hacarbon per ha at the cleared sites, pre-clearing (CTrees 68 Mg/ha + roots) 240,263 tCO₂e/yr baseline
× 50% effectivenessshare of that clearing the project actually averts 120,131 t/yr
× (1−20%) leakageemissions displaced elsewhere 96,105 t/yr
× (1−15%) uncertaintyVMD0055 deduction (shrinks with field plots) 81,689 t/yr
× (1−15%) buffernon-permanence buffer withheld by the registry ≈ 69,436 credits/yr
In one line: 1,616 ha/yr × 145 tCO₂e/ha × 50% × 80% × 85% × 85% ≈ 69,436 credits/yr. The baseline (240,263 tCO₂e/yr) is real — GFW clearing × CTrees carbon. Note the carbon at cleared sites (~68 Mg/ha) is about half the reserve mean: clearing eats the accessible edges first. Carbon prices below ($4–$20/tonne) span the voluntary market range.
